ety.text: From Middle English dale, from Old English dæl, from Proto-West Germanic *dal, from Proto-Germanic *dalą.
Related to Low German daal or Dutch daal (“lowers, descends”) and French dalle (“trough; conduit”). Attested in English since the seventeenth century.

senses.d: A valley, often in an otherwise hilly area.
ex: And we will all the pleasures prove / That hills and valleys, dales and fields, / Woods, or steepy mountain yields
Over hill, over dale / As we hit the dusty trail, / And those caissons go rolling along.

senses.d: The sunken or grooved portion of the surface of a vinyl record.
A trough or spout to carry off water, as from a pump.
ex: The pump-dale scupper is that to which the dale leads, that conveys the water from the pumps to the side on the lower deck of large ships.

ety.text: From Latin vallem, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Sicilian vaḍḍuni.
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin vallem, with a change in gender.
From Old Galician-Portuguese vale, val, from Latin vallis (“valley”).
